nameStory: Small-flowered winter-cress gets its name from two key traits: its tiny yellow flowers that are noticeably smaller than its relatives, and its ability to stay green through winter like watercress. The 'cress' part comes from an old Germanic word meaning 'to creep or crawl,' referring to how these plants spread along the ground.
description: Small-flowered winter-cress is a low-growing member of the mustard family that forms leafy rosettes close to the ground. This hardy little plant typically grows 6-18 inches tall when flowering, with deeply lobed leaves that stay green even in winter. Its small, bright yellow flowers bloom in loose clusters above the foliage, followed by slender seed pods that point upward like tiny green fingers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers with four petals arranged in a cross shape, noticeably smaller than other wintercresses - each flower is only about 1/8 inch across and feels delicate to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided leaves with rounded lobes that feel smooth and slightly waxy, arranged in a flat rosette that hugs the ground - the leaves have a mild peppery taste when crushed

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Slender, upright seed pods (siliques) that are 1-2 inches long and feel firm when mature, splitting open to reveal tiny round seeds arranged in two rows

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading rosettes that stay close to the ground, with flowering stems that rise up from the center - the whole plant feels sturdy and slightly succulent

idTips.label: Winter Leaves
idTips.description: Remains green and fresh-looking through winter when most other plants have died back, with leaves that feel thick and cold-resistant to the touch

habitat: Look for small-flowered winter-cress in moist, disturbed soils along stream banks, wet meadows, and roadside ditches throughout New England. It thrives in areas that stay damp but not waterlogged, often growing alongside skunk cabbage, jewelweed, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll also find it in garden beds and waste areas where the soil has been turned over.

seasonality.spring: Bright yellow flower clusters appear in April and May, making this the easiest time for identification. The fresh green rosettes become more prominent as they prepare to send up flowering stems.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and are replaced by upright seed pods that gradually turn from green to brown. The basal leaves remain green and can still be spotted among taller summer vegetation.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods split open to release seeds, and the plant begins forming fresh rosettes for winter. New growth appears bright green against the browning landscape.
seasonality.winter: One of the few plants that stays vibrant green under snow, with thick rosettes of deeply lobed leaves that can be spotted even in frozen ground.

funFact: Small-flowered winter-cress is like nature's refrigerator vegetable - it actually gets sweeter and more tender after being exposed to frost, as the cold weather converts starches in the leaves into sugars as a natural antifreeze!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its larger cousin bitter wintercress, but small-flowered winter-cress has noticeably tinier flowers that you could easily cover with your pinky nail. Memory trick: 'Small name, small flowers' - if the flowers look proportionally large for a wintercress, it's probably not this one.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'cress,' this plant is not closely related to watercress that you might find in grocery stores, though both belong to the mustard family and have that characteristic peppery bite. The wintercresses are sometimes called 'land cresses' to distinguish them from their aquatic cousins.
compareHints: Small-flowered winter-cress stands out from other wintercresses primarily by its diminutive flowers - they're about half the size of bitter wintercress blooms. Compared to American yellowrocket, it has a more compact growth habit and stays closer to the ground. Land cress has more rounded, less deeply divided leaves and tends to grow in more consistently wet areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bitter wintercress has the largest, most rounded terminal leaf lobe compared to its relatives.
Land cress differs from bitter wintercress by having more rounded, less deeply cut leaf lobes and a milder flavor.
Among its wintercress relatives in New England, American yellowrocket is distinguished by its more compact growth habit and distinctly oval, less-divided leaves.
